column5: exalt the Lord’s name together
column6: The commentary commands praise of the Lord’s high name; in David’s psalm the worshippers are told to magnify YHWH together and exalt his name together, a direct communal formulation.

column5: name praised from sunrise to sunset
column6: The commentary joins the Lord’s name to praise; this hymn says the Lord’s name is to be praised from the rising of the sun to its setting, extending the act across the whole day.

column5: glory due the name and offerings in the courts
column6: The commentary links raised houses, the Lord’s name, and worship; the psalm tells worshippers to ascribe glory to the Lord’s name and bring an offering into his courts.

column5: chosen sanctuary where God places his name
column6: The commentary cites houses authorized for worship with the Lord’s name in them; Deuteronomy commands Israel to seek the place God chooses for his name and dwelling, supplying the covenant sanctuary background.

column5: altar and remembered name
column6: The commentary links remembering the Lord’s name with prayer; God says he will come and bless at every altar where he causes his name to be remembered, joining invocation to sacrifice.

column5: great name among nations and pure offering
column6: The commentary ties praise of the Lord’s name to worship in houses; Malachi says the Lord’s name is great among the nations and that offerings are made to it across the earth.

column5: glorious name exalted above blessing and praise
column6: The commentary commands exaltation of the Lord’s name; the Levites’ public prayer blesses God’s glorious name, exalted above all blessing and praise.

column5: blessed name in bereavement
column6: The commentary defines tasbih as declaring God free of every evil; after losing his children and possessions Job blesses the Lord’s name, showing praise under calamity rather than only in prosperity.

column5: blessed name, kings raised and removed
column6: The commentary contrasts God’s true height with a ruler’s claim; Daniel blesses God’s name forever because wisdom and might belong to him and he removes and sets up kings.

column5: Most High rules human kingdoms
column6: The commentary’s Pharaoh claims supreme rule for himself; the heavenly decree in Daniel says the Most High rules the kingdom of humanity and gives it to whom he wills, framing Nebuchadnezzar’s later boast and humbling.

column5: kingdom taken during the king’s boast
column6: The commentary presents Pharaoh’s “I am the highest lord” as a creature’s false claim; Daniel’s heavenly voice interrupts Nebuchadnezzar’s boast and announces that his kingship has departed from him.

column5: the Lord descends and proclaims his name
column6: The commentary calls for praise of the Lord’s name; at Sinai the Lord descends in a cloud and proclaims the divine name before Moses, giving the naming formula a theophanic setting.

column5: name proclaimed through merciful attributes
column6: The commentary defines tasbih as denying every evil of God; the proclamation following the name calls the Lord merciful, gracious, patient, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.

column5: light of the Lord’s face
column6: The commentary’s cited expression about the radiance, majesty, and light of the Lord’s face has a close benediction parallel: the priest asks that the Lord make his face shine upon Israel.

column5: prayer for the light of God’s face
column6: The commentary connects the Lord’s face with glory and light; the psalmist prays for the light of God’s face to shine upon the worshippers, making the image explicitly devotional.

column5: seeing God’s face and the limit of mortal life
column6: The commentary cites language about the Lord’s face as overwhelming glory and light; when Moses asks to see God’s glory, Exodus says no human can see God’s face and live, setting a distinct boundary around that face imagery.

column5: glory appearing as devouring fire on the mountain
column6: The commentary connects divine majesty and light with the great fire; at Sinai the Lord’s glory appears to Israel like a devouring fire on the mountain’s summit, joining height, glory, and fire.

column5: the Lord as consuming fire
column6: The commentary names the great fire in the judgment scene; Moses warns Israel that the Lord their God is a consuming fire, so the fire image also expresses divine holiness and judgment.

column5: Hannah’s exaltation and praise
column6: The commentary pairs the Lord’s exaltation with a worshipper’s prayer; Hannah says her strength is exalted in the Lord and rejoices in his salvation, placing elevation in grateful devotion rather than self-claim.

column5: God brings low and raises up
column6: The commentary makes highness and lowliness opposite ends of one axis; Hannah’s prayer says the Lord makes poor and rich and brings low and raises up.

column5: the needy raised from dust to sit with princes
column6: The commentary describes the chosen life as low and lesser; Hannah says God lifts the needy from the dust and seats them with princes, a concrete reversal of low status.

column5: God raises the humble and casts down the wicked
column6: The commentary contrasts true divine elevation with a ruler’s arrogance; the psalm says the Lord raises the humble and casts the wicked down, assigning the upward and downward movement to God.

column5: God puts one down and lifts another
column6: The commentary treats elevation as the Lord’s rightful attribute and worldly self-exaltation as false; the psalm calls God the judge who brings one down and raises another.

column5: Hebrew kabbir and Arabic k-b-r
column6: The commentary labels ٱلْكُبْرَىٰ with k-b-r and explains tekbir as declaring God great; Job calls God kabbir, “mighty,” attesting a related Semitic greatness word, though the Hebrew verse emphasizes might.

column5: one king over earth and one name
column6: The commentary praises the Lord as highest and links the name to worship; Zechariah says YHWH will be king over all the earth and his name one, uniting universal rule with the divine name.

column5: Hebrew shem and Arabic ism in the self-made name
column6: The commentary labels ٱسْمَ as a name whose mention is raised; Babel’s builders seek to make a shem for themselves while raising a tower toward heaven. Hebrew shem is cognate with Arabic ism, though the Hebrew verse does not derive it from height.

column5: Hebrew shem and Arabic ism in praise
column6: The commentary labels ٱسْمَ as the name that raises the named one’s remembrance; the psalm calls YHWH’s shem majestic throughout the earth. The cognate appears in a praise formula, without importing the commentary’s proposed etymology.

column5: morning star fallen from heaven
column6: The commentary develops a silhouette rising above the horizon and a ruler’s claimed height; Isaiah addresses a fallen morning star before recounting the speaker’s ascent and boast, adding a celestial image to the self-exaltation scene.

column5: throne glory, streams of fire, and unapproachable face
column6: The commentary’s gloss connects the Lord’s facial radiance and majesty with light and fire; Enoch’s heavenly throne vision joins fiery streams to overwhelming glory and a face no flesh can behold.

column5: God scatters the proud
column6: The commentary treats Pharaoh’s claim to highest rank as arrogance; Mary’s hymn says God scatters the proud in the intention of their hearts, adding the divine reversal of self-exaltation.

column5: treasure reveals the heart’s allegiance
column6: The commentary says people choose the low and near life; Jesus says the heart follows its treasure, making the preference for earthly life an inward allegiance rather than a mere circumstance.

column5: choice between God and wealth
column6: The commentary names a choice of the lower, nearer life; Jesus says no one can serve both God and mammon, making that preference a direct choice of master.

column5: Paul reads Pharaoh’s role as serving God’s name
column6: The commentary presents Pharaoh’s “highest lord” claim as false human elevation; Paul quotes Exodus to say Pharaoh was raised up so God’s power and name would be proclaimed, interpreting the same ruler as an instrument of divine sovereignty.

column5: God’s glory shines in Christ’s face
column6: The commentary’s gloss joins radiance and light to the Lord’s face; Paul describes the knowledge of God’s glory in the face of Christ, with light shining in human hearts.

column5: visible transient things and unseen eternal things
column6: The commentary hears al-dunya as the nearer, lesser life and the surah contrasts it with what lasts; Paul says visible things are temporary while unseen things are eternal.

column5: trying to save life and losing it
column6: The commentary warns that people prefer the low, near life; Jesus says whoever seeks to save life will lose it, while whoever loses life for his sake will save it.

column5: set the mind above, not on earth
column6: The commentary sets the high against the near earthly life; Paul commands believers to seek the things above rather than things on earth, stating that orientation directly.

column5: earthly-mindedness as the road to destruction
column6: The commentary calls the chosen earthly life low and nearer; Paul describes people whose minds are set on earthly things and whose end is destruction, supplying a concrete moral consequence.

column5: citizenship in heaven
column6: The commentary’s axis contrasts the near life with a higher enduring orientation; Paul says believers’ citizenship is in heaven, naming the alternative to earthly-mindedness.

column5: God as consuming fire in a call to worship
column6: The commentary links divine majesty and the great fire; Hebrews urges reverent worship because God is a consuming fire, bringing the image into a Christian liturgical warning.

column5: Satan falls from heaven
column6: The commentary sets true divine height against a creature’s arrogant claim; Jesus says he saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning, a specific heavenly fall that resonates with the descent of Isaiah’s self-exalting figure.

column5: Mary’s “magnifying” as the soul’s reception of God
column6: The commentary says the name raises the named one’s remembrance; Origen’s homily on Mary’s Magnificat explains her soul’s magnifying of the Lord as a change in the human recipient’s capacity to perceive and receive God, not an increase in God’s greatness.
